query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale multilayer coatings composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy (HEA) layers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by an interplay between lattice misfit‐induced interface stability and strain‐driven evolution of short-range order (SRO). Under load, the inherent lattice distortions in these HEA multilayers cause periodic disruption and partial reformation of SRO at the interfaces, which modulates dislocation nucleation and mobility. This interplay produces an initial low creep rate that gradually localizes strain at the interfaces (via intermittent dislocation pinning and unpinning) as plastic deformation evolves.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating with alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers that exhibit severe lattice distortion and intrinsic SRO at their interfaces.
generation.intervention: Application of a constant, sustained mechanical load (at moderate, controlled elevated temperatures) that maintains the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
generation.conditions: Isothermal conditions at a temperature that is high enough to permit thermally activated dislocation processes but low enough to avoid rapid diffusion-induced phase changes; an applied stress level near the onset of plasticity that allows gradual accumulation of strain.
generation.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC interface regions—with their lattice misfit and localized SRO—mediates dislocation transmission by periodically pinning and releasing defects during progressive deformation.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate within the strained, distorted lattice and move toward the multilayer interfaces. Here, the existing SRO is partially disrupted by strain, reducing local barriers to dislocation motion and triggering a temporary increase in creep. However, dynamic reordering (or strain-induced SRO evolution) then occurs at the interface, re-establishing obstacles that slow further dislocation glide. The balance between these competing effects—stable, moderately negative lattice misfit that reinforces the interface and the strain-induced degradation/reformation of SRO—governs the progressive plastic deformation response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a monolithic HEA with uniform composition, the multilayer structure will initially exhibit lower creep strain due to interfacial pinning. Over time, as sustained load induces local SRO degradation and enhanced dislocation activity near interfaces, localized shear bands and increased dislocation density will appear, causing a gradual acceleration in the creep rate. This transition, observable via in situ TEM and nanoindentation tests, would be distinct from the more homogeneous deformation seen in conventional multilayers.
generation.baseline: Monolithic or bulk HEA films without engineered nanoscale layering, which exhibit more homogeneous plastic flow and less pronounced strain localization under similar loading conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold when the multilayer periodicity is maintained in the nanoscale regime (layer thickness < ~100 nm) and under stress/temperature conditions where diffusion remains limited so that dislocation-mediated processes and SRO evolution dominate. Extreme conditions that trigger full phase transformation or diffusion-driven processes may fall outside this model.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., PMC12964539::web::000 on dislocation activity in refractory HEAs and PMC12842692::web::025 on lattice misfit effects in HE superalloys) support the role of lattice distortion and interfacial stability in controlling deformation, the precise contribution of dynamic SRO evolution in multilayer environments remains uncertain and awaits direct observation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate HEA nanoscale multilayers with controlled variations in interface lattice misfit (e.g., by adjusting layer compositions) and pre-characterized SRO levels (via tailored heat treatments). Perform in situ TEM and nanoindentation creep tests under sustained loading at a fixed moderate temperature, while comparing with monolithic HEA films.
measurements: Evolution of dislocation density and motion (observed by in situ TEM)
Local SRO assessment at interfaces (using techniques like 4D-STEM or high-resolution diffraction)
Mapping of localized deformation (shear band formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayers do not exhibit a noticeable shift from homogeneous deformation to localized strain build-up at the interfaces (i.e., if dislocation activity and creep rates do not correlate with changes in SRO or lattice misfit variations), then the mechanistic role of interface-mediated SRO evolution in governing progressive plastic deformation would be falsified.
